title: Importing Data
text:
Once your audio and annotation files are ready (see Preparing Your Data), the next step is to bring them into DeepAcoustics. This page covers two parts of that process: importing a Raven selection table so DeepAcoustics saves it as a detections .mat file, and adjusting the display settings so you can see and navigate your data.


Importing a Raven Selection Table
DeepAcoustics does not work directly from Raven selection tables. Instead, it converts them into its own detections file format (.mat), which is what you load for review, training, and testing.

Open the Raven import. Go to File > Import / Export > Import from Raven.
Answer the Multi-Raven Import prompt. A dialog asks whether you are importing multiple Raven tables and/or audio files, or only one table and its one audio file:

Yes - I have multiple tables and/or audio files: the option you will choose most of the time.
No - I am doing only one table and its one audio file: a legacy option from DeepSqueak, which could only import single audio files. It can still be useful if you are working with one long audio file.


Select the selection table. Navigate to the Raven selection table (.txt) containing your annotations or test data, and select it.
Select the audio folder. DeepAcoustics then asks for the folder containing the audio files that go with the selection table. Select that folder and click OK. DeepAcoustics always asks for this folder during import, even if you selected an audio folder earlier. Additionally, you will be prompted to select an audio file to load. You will be able to navigate to and load the other files, but this is indicating where you want to start in your review:
Save the detections file. Finally, DeepAcoustics asks where to save the new detections file. By default, the file name is built from the name of the first audio file, the total number of audio files, and _Detections.mat. For example:
HYDBBA103OOI_170108-133500_24AudFiles_Detections.mat
If a file with the same name already exists in that location, it will be overwritten.







TipName your .mat files clearly



DeepAcoustics saves several kinds of files with the same .mat extension, including detections files and training image files. Suffixes such as _Detections and _Images help, but it is worth adding a clear prefix or suffix of your own so you can always tell what a file contains. For example, adding Annotations to the name of a file of manually annotated calls (such as Train_Annotations.mat) separates it from a file of detections produced by a network.





Visualizing the Data
Once the detections file is saved, you can load it and adjust the display to suit your calls.

Loading the detections file

Load the detections. Go to File > Load Detections (see GUI Overview) and choose your detections file. If your file has a single call type, it will simply open. If there are multiple call types, a dialog lists the call types in the file and lets you choose which ones to load. See the next section about Annotation Review for how to best use this feature.
Choose a starting audio file. DeepAcoustics asks which audio file to load. This only sets where in the dataset you start; all the other audio files remain available. In most cases, select the first audio file in the folder and click OK.








Important



If you save your session afterward without changing the detections file’s name, DeepAcoustics will overwrite the existing file, keeping only the call types you selected when loading it. To keep the complete original file, save your session under a new file name instead.




Adjusting the display settings
When you first load a detections file, the spectrogram may still use settings from the last file you loaded, or the default settings. For example, if you last reviewed blue whale calls and are now loading dolphin detections, the display will still be set up for blue whales. You will usually need to adjust the controls in the Settings panel before your calls display well.
Focus and Page durations

Focus: sets the duration shown in the upper (focus) spectrogram. A value of around 30 seconds is a good starting point for getting an overall sense of a file. You can then shorten or lengthen it to zoom in or out, depending on your calls and what you want to see.
Page: sets the duration shown in the lower (page) spectrogram panel. It works well to set this to the length of your audio files, for example 600 seconds for a 10-minute file or 300 seconds for a 5-minute file. You can then see where all the annotations fall within the file.

Detections are also marked along the very bottom of the window. The green density plot shows where detections are concentrated within the loaded file.





The controls for the focus and page time scales are adjacent to the color map tools. For both of the focus and page screens, a user can either define a duration to display, or select from a few pre-set settings.





Display Settings
Select Display Settings to open the spectrogram settings dialog. When you click OK, the spectrograms are redrawn with the new settings and the color limits are recalculated.

Frequency Lower Limit (Hz) and Frequency Upper Limit (Hz): the range of frequencies shown on the spectrogram, in Hz. The lower limit must be less than the upper limit, and the highest frequency that can be displayed is half the sampling rate. For example, the example file has a 2000 Hz sampling rate, so the upper limit is set to 1000 Hz.
Spectrogram Units: the units of the values plotted in the spectrogram, which are also shown on the color bar beside it.

Amplitude: the magnitude of each time and frequency bin of the spectrogram (the default).
Power Spectral Density: the power in each bin, normalized by the sampling rate and the window, and shown on a logarithmic (dB) scale. This can make faint calls easier to see against background noise.

Units of Spectrogram Parameters: whether Window Size and NFFT are entered as a number of Samples or as a duration in Seconds. The two are equivalent (seconds = samples ÷ sampling rate). Seconds can be convenient when you work with files at different sampling rates, because the same duration gives the same time resolution.
Window Size: the length of each chunk of audio that is analyzed to create one column of the spectrogram. Longer windows give finer frequency resolution but blur rapid changes in time; shorter windows show timing more sharply but blur frequency. Long, low-frequency tonal calls (such as blue and fin whale calls) generally suit longer windows, while short or fast-changing calls (such as clicks and whistles) suit shorter windows.
Overlap (%): how much each window overlaps the next. Higher overlap produces a smoother spectrogram along the time axis but takes longer to compute. It must be less than 95%.
NFFT: the number of points used in the Fourier transform of each window, which sets the spacing between frequency bins (sampling rate ÷ NFFT). It is usually set equal to the window size. Setting it larger than the window size pads the window with zeros, which smooths the spectrogram’s appearance without adding true frequency resolution.
Auto Window Size: calculates a window size (and sets NFFT to the same value) so that the spectrogram’s pixels are roughly square, based on the current Focus duration, the frequency limits, and the overlap. It is a quick starting point when you aren’t sure what to use. Audio must be loaded first, because the calculation needs the sampling rate.

Color Map and color limits
The spectrogram is drawn by mapping each value (amplitude or power) to a color in the color map, using MATLAB’s color limits:

Low Color Limit: any value at or below this limit is drawn in the lowest (darkest) color of the color map.
High Color Limit: any value at or above this limit is drawn in the highest (brightest) color.
In between: values that fall between the two limits are spread evenly across the colors in between.

When the display is updated, DeepAcoustics sets the starting limits automatically from the spectrogram itself, using the 10th and 90th percentiles of its values. Each click of + or - then moves that limit by 10% of the current range:

Raising the Low Color Limit (+) pushes more of the quieter background into the darkest color, so the background looks darker and calls stand out more.
Lowering the High Color Limit (-) makes more values reach the brightest color, so faint calls appear brighter. If you lower it too far, strong calls saturate and lose detail.
Moving both limits closer together increases the contrast; moving them apart reduces it.

When Spectrogram Units is set to Amplitude, the Low Color Limit cannot go below zero.

Color Map: the set of colors used to draw the spectrogram (for example, inferno). Choose a different color map, or use the button beside it to invert the current one, to find what works best for viewing your data.




Navigating through the data
DeepAcoustics offers several ways to move through your dataset, depending on what you are trying to do:

Audio file selector: at the top of the upper (focus) spectrogram, you can select a different audio file and go straight to it.
Navigation panel: at the bottom of the window, buttons move you to the next or previous call, or forward and back through the spectrogram by a small step or a full page.
File buttons (pink): these move to the next or previous audio file, or to the next or previous audio file that contains a call.
Go to a specific call: in the upper left corner, type an annotation number to jump directly to that call. This is useful for returning to where you left off when reviewing or annotating.

title: Network Architectures, Hyperparameters & Performance Metrics
text:
This page lays out the technical building blocks referenced throughout the rest of the guide: the network architectures DeepAcoustics offers, the hyperparameters you can tune when training one, and the metrics used to evaluate how well a trained network performs. The hands-on, step-by-step process of actually creating training images, training a network, and running performance tests in DeepAcoustics is covered separately under Network Training & Testing; this page is the conceptual reference those steps point back to.


Available architectures
DeepAcoustics offers three pre-trained YOLOv4 backbone architectures. TinyYOLO and CSP-DarkNet-53 are pre-trained on COCO, a segmentation-based database of over 330,000 object images; ResNet-50 is pre-trained on ImageNet, a bounding-box-based database of roughly 1.5 million images.

TinyYOLO is the lightest and fastest to train, making it the natural starting point for optimizing other settings before moving to the larger architectures. CSP-DarkNet-53 is the largest and most complex of the three, with roughly five times TinyYOLO’s parameter count and an additional detection head. ResNet-50 sits in between, and additionally requires a fixed 224×224 input resolution (TinyYOLO and CSP-DarkNet-53 instead require an input resolution that is a multiple of 32 pixels).






NoteGuide media placeholder



Short clip or annotated image walking through the trade-offs between the three architectures. To be added once available.





Key hyperparameters
Training behavior is governed by a handful of settings a user can tune:

Learning rate: controls how large a step the network takes when updating its weights after each training batch. Values of 0.0001, 0.0005, 0.001, and 0.002 have all been tested; too high a rate can cause unstable training, too low can make training impractically slow.
Batch / mini-batch size: the number of training images processed together before each weight update. Values from 16 up to 512 have been tested; larger batches use more GPU memory but can produce more stable gradient estimates.
Epochs: the number of complete passes through the training dataset. Training is typically monitored via a loss curve (below) to judge when additional epochs stop helping.
Optimizer: the algorithm used to update network weights (e.g., sgdm, RMSProp, adam in MATLAB’s implementation); different optimizers can affect convergence speed and stability.
Validation split: the percentage of training data automatically held back each epoch to monitor performance on unseen data during training, rather than supplying a separate validation folder. The reference network used an 18% automatic split.






How to read a training/validation loss curve: both curves falling together (underfitting; more training may help), both low and stable (good fit), or validation loss rising while training loss keeps falling (overfitting; stop near the point where validation loss is lowest).

Anchor boxes
YOLO-family networks don’t draw each bounding box from scratch. Instead, they start from a small set of ready-made box shapes called anchor boxes and learn how to move and stretch the closest shape so it fits each call. DeepAcoustics works out the anchor shapes from the bounding boxes in your own training annotations (using MATLAB’s estimateAnchorBoxes, which groups your boxes by width and height). The anchors therefore reflect the real shapes of your calls rather than generic defaults.





The animation above shows the process in four steps:

Divide the spectrogram into a grid. The network splits each spectrogram image into a grid of squares. Every square looks for calls at the same time, in a single pass through the network.
Start from a few box shapes. Each square has the same small set of anchor box shapes (for example, tall, medium, long, and small), centered on that square. Their sizes come from the calls you annotated. The shapes do not slide or scan across the image: every square and every shape is evaluated at the same time, in one pass.
Move and stretch the closest shape to fit the call. The square that contains the center of a call takes the anchor shape that most closely matches the call, then shifts it and stretches it wider, narrower, taller, or shorter so it fits the call. The final box does not have to match the anchor’s original size.
Keep the best box. Every square makes a guess, and each guess comes with a confidence score from 0 (unlikely) to 1 (very likely). Squares that contain only background noise make guesses too, but these score low. Squares next to a call often make overlapping guesses at the same call. Guesses below the confidence threshold are dropped, and where several boxes overlap the same call, only the highest-scoring box is kept.


Common questions

How does the network know how to fit a call? It learns this during training. For every square and every anchor shape, the network outputs a confidence score, a call type, and four adjustments (shift left or right, shift up or down, stretch wider or narrower, and stretch taller or shorter). During training, each annotated call is assigned to the square that contains its center and the anchor shape that most closely matches it, and the network is corrected based on how close its adjustments come to your annotation. After many examples, it learns what your calls look like in the image and how to box them.
Is there a call in every square? No. Most squares contain only background noise and learn to give a very low confidence score, meaning “nothing here.” A square only needs to contain the center of a call, and the box it predicts can extend well beyond the square’s edges. This is how a single square can produce a box around a long call.
Does a square only see its own small patch of the image? No. A square is the center point for its anchor boxes, and the boxes can extend across many neighboring squares. Each square’s prediction is also based on a much larger area of the image around it, so it can take in the whole call. Neighboring squares have their own set of anchor boxes, centered on themselves.
What are the low-scoring boxes on empty noise? Every square makes a guess, including the many squares that contain only background noise, so guesses can land anywhere in the image, not just near calls. A well-trained network gives these very low scores, and the confidence threshold removes them. When something in the noise looks enough like a call to score above the threshold, it becomes a false positive.
Do overlapping boxes get merged? Not exactly. The overlapping boxes are not averaged together. After low-confidence boxes are removed, a step called non-maximum suppression keeps the single highest-scoring box wherever boxes overlap the same call and discards the rest.



Anchor box details in DeepAcoustics

What an anchor is: a fixed width and height. Anchors describe shape only; where a call sits in the image is handled by the grid, not by the anchors.
How anchors are divided: DeepAcoustics sorts the anchors by area and splits them across the network’s detection heads, each of which uses its own grid. TinyYOLO and ResNet-50 each have two heads: the larger half of the anchors goes to a coarse grid, which suits large calls, and the smaller half goes to a finer grid, which suits small calls. CSP-DarkNet-53 has three heads and splits the anchors into thirds.
Valid anchor counts: TinyYOLO and ResNet-50 need an even number of anchors, and CSP-DarkNet-53 needs a multiple of three. If you enter a count that doesn’t fit, DeepAcoustics rounds it up to the next valid number (for example, 11 becomes 12 on TinyYOLO). The defaults are 8 anchors for TinyYOLO and ResNet-50 and 9 for CSP-DarkNet-53.



Choosing the number of anchor boxes

What changes with more or fewer anchors: More anchors give each square more starting shapes, so there is more likely to be a close match for calls of unusual shapes (very long, very short, or broadband). The network then needs smaller adjustments and tends to fit boxes more tightly. Fewer anchors are faster and lighter, but a call that is far from every shape needs a large stretch, which is harder to learn and can lead to looser boxes or missed calls.
Use the mean IoU curve: When you choose Customize during training and don’t already know how many anchors you want, DeepAcoustics plots mean IoU against the number of anchors (1 to 15). Mean IoU measures how well the anchor shapes match your annotated boxes. Choose the smallest number of anchors that still gives an acceptably high mean IoU, which is usually near the bend (or “elbow”) of the curve, where adding more anchors stops improving the fit much.
Match the count to call variability: The more your calls vary in duration, bandwidth, and aspect ratio, the more anchors you are likely to need to box them accurately. This matters most for multiclass networks that combine long and short call types. In testing, moving to 8 anchors improved a multiclass network, and higher anchor counts increased recall for sei whale calls.
Watch the costs: More anchors increase computation and memory use and can lead to overfitting. Higher anchor counts (such as 10) have caused training runs to crash on some machines but not others, possibly because of memory limits, so try a machine with more RAM before ruling a configuration out.
Comparing architectures: Because the architectures have different numbers of detection heads, keep the total number of anchors as close as possible when comparing them, rather than the number per head. For example, 6 anchors on TinyYOLO compares to 6 on CSP-DarkNet-53; 8 or 10 compares to 9; and 12 compares to 12.
Resolution changes the anchors: Anchors are estimated in the pixel dimensions of the resized training images, so training at a different image resolution produces different anchors even when the anchor count stays the same. Keep this in mind when comparing networks trained at different input sizes.




Variability across training runs
Because random factors (weight initialization, data shuffling, augmentation draws) influence each training run, the same TinyYOLO configuration was trained three independent times in developing the reference network, and each resulting network evaluated separately, to characterize how much performance varies for reasons unrelated to the chosen hyperparameters. This context is useful when comparing two configurations that differ only slightly in a performance metric. A difference smaller than the run-to-run variability isn’t necessarily meaningful.




Performance metrics

Intersection over Union (IoU)
IoU measures how much a predicted bounding box overlaps a ground-truth (manually annotated) box. It is calculated as the area of their overlap divided by the area of their union. A higher IoU threshold demands tighter overlap and is therefore a stricter detection criterion.





IoU = (area of overlap) / (area of union). DeepAcoustics’ default true-positive threshold is a fairly permissive IoU ≥ 0.1; mAP then summarizes performance across a range of stricter IoU cutoffs (0.1 to 0.9).


Precision, recall, and F1-score
DeepAcoustics’ built-in performance evaluation compares network detections against a ground-truth annotation file. Predicted boxes are produced at a 0.5 confidence threshold by default (MATLAB’s YOLOv4 default), and a detection counts as a true positive if its IoU with a ground-truth box is at least 0.1.

Precision: the proportion of the network’s detections that were correct (true positives ÷ all detections).
Recall: the proportion of actual annotated calls the network successfully detected (true positives ÷ all ground-truth calls).
F1-score: the harmonic mean of precision and recall at the 0.5 confidence threshold, giving equal weight to both and penalizing large gaps between them more than a simple average would.



Average precision (AP) and mean average precision (mAP)
A single confidence threshold only tells part of the story, so DeepAcoustics also computes average precision (AP) across the full range of confidence thresholds from 0.5 to 1, at the fixed 0.1 IoU threshold, summarizing the precision/recall trade-off as the confidence cutoff is varied. Mean average precision (mAP) goes a step further, repeating that AP calculation at nine IoU thresholds from 0.1 to 0.9 (in 10% increments) and averaging the results, which captures both how completely calls are detected and how tightly the predicted boxes fit them.





Matches the style of DeepAcoustics’ own performance-evaluation output: each point is one confidence (score) threshold, colored by that threshold’s value, with average precision shown in the title. (Example data shown, not a real evaluation run.) AP is the area under this curve at one IoU threshold; mAP averages AP across several IoU thresholds.
Because the “Noise” class exists only as a training-time workaround for a MATLAB datastore limitation (true negatives can’t otherwise be included in training), performance metrics are not meaningful for, and are not reported on, that class.
